# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
**Northgate Progress Institute**
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
**October 2026**

## Executive summary

- 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023, an average of one person roughly every 11 minutes. A toll that size is not an accident of American life. It is the product of two gaps in federal law that Congress wrote and that Congress can close.
- 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and they are back on the civilian market.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023. That is one American killed roughly every 11 minutes, around the clock, for an entire year. It is more than 125 deaths a day, every day, weekends and holidays included.

A number this large stops meaning anything unless we make it mean something. So start with what each of those deaths actually is: an emptied desk in a classroom, an empty chair at a dinner table, a shift that no one covers. Then multiply it across 46,728 families, and add the classrooms, workplaces, churches and grocery stores where whole communities learned a new set of dates.

It is tempting to treat a toll like this as weather, something that simply happens to the United States. It is not weather. It runs through specific choices, and two of them frame everything else in this brief. Congress chose to let a large share of gun sales proceed with no background check at all, and in 2004 Congress chose to let the assault weapons ban expire. Both choices have a body count attached, and both are reversible.

The annual toll is not a plateau we should learn to live with. It is the running total of a policy failure that has a cure written into it: close the gaps.

## 2. Children and teens

Nowhere is the cost stated more plainly than among children. In 2023, 2,566 children were shot and killed in the United States. That is about seven children every day, a school bus's worth of loss by the end of a month.

Children in America are shot and killed at a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children, ahead of car crashes and every other cause. Read that sentence again, because it has stopped shocking anyone, and it should not. In no other wealthy country is the leading threat to a child's life something that Congress could take off the market.

The usual explanations do not survive contact with the data. American children are not uniquely reckless. Our cities are not uniquely violent. What distinguishes the United States is the sheer availability of guns, including the guns most often used to kill, and availability is a policy choice. Nothing about childhood here requires a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. That number was built, and it can be unbuilt.

Every year that Congress leaves the background check gap and the assault weapons gap open, the tally of children shot and killed starts over. The 2,566 children killed in 2023 will not be in anyone's class photo this fall. Their classmates will carry the absence for the rest of their lives.

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic gate in American gun safety law. Since the Brady law took effect in 1994, anyone buying from a licensed dealer is screened for the disqualifying records federal law already recognizes: felony convictions, domestic violence, and the other categories that Congress has long barred from buying guns.

But the gate only covers some doors, and that is the problem. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged online, at gun shows and between strangers routinely bypass the system entirely. A buyer who would fail a check at a licensed counter can answer an ad, meet a private seller in a parking lot and drive away armed. For someone with a disqualifying record, the workaround is not a hindrance. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks close exactly this gap, and nothing else. The policy is simple: every sale runs through the same system, whoever the seller is. No new categories of prohibited person, no new register, just the same check applied to every purchase that already carries one when a licensed dealer is involved. It is the gun safety measure with the longest track record of bipartisan support at the state level, and the one Congress has debated for more than a decade without closing.

The gap has a cost we can count. Every year it stays open, some share of those 46,728 deaths is a sale that a completed check would have stopped. There is no version of this argument where leaving 40% of the market outside the system is the safer option.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 delivered 656 of them, shootings like Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023. Each of those words is now a place name that stands for a specific afternoon, a specific set of families, and a specific set of unfinished lives.

For the communities that lived through them, nothing here is abstract. And what connects many of the deadliest of these attacks is the weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. They are designed to put a high volume of fire into human beings quickly, with detachable magazines that let a shooter keep firing while people flee. They have no purpose on a civilian street that justifies what they do in a school hallway.

The country has already run this experiment in the right direction. The 1994 assault weapons ban prohibited the manufacture and sale of these weapons for the civilian market, and it lasted a decade before Congress let it lapse in 2004. Since then the industry has marketed aggressively around the memory of the ban, selling military-style rifles and large-capacity magazines to a civilian customer base, and the results show up in the mass shooting count year after year.

Reinstating the ban is not nostalgia. An updated ban would cover the copycat designs the industry developed to route around the 1994 definitions, and would reach the large-capacity magazines that make these weapons so lethal in crowded places. Congress has the 1994 law as a drafting template and more than two decades of evidence about what the industry did with the gap.

## 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every gun sale, with no exception for private sales, online sales or gun show sales, so that the same standard applies whoever the seller is.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban, extend it to the copycat designs marketed since 2004, and restrict the large-capacity magazines that make these weapons so deadly in crowded places.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, and require that the findings be published so that states and cities can act on them.
4. **Help states adopt extreme-risk laws.** Create grant incentives for state extreme-risk, or red flag, laws that allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove guns from a person in crisis.

The two gaps at the center of this brief were made by Congress. That is the good news, because what Congress made, Congress can unmake. The toll of 2023 is already written into the data. What the data look like next year, and every year after, is the part that is still up for a vote. Seven children a day are waiting on the answer.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
**Northgate Progress Institute**
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
**October 2026**

## Executive summary

- 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023, one death roughly every 11 minutes. A toll that size is not an accident of American life. It is the product of two gaps in federal law that Congress wrote and that Congress can close.
- 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and they are back on the civilian market.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help states adopt extreme-risk laws. Every one of these steps is ready for a vote.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023. That is one American killed roughly every 11 minutes, around the clock, for an entire year. It is more than 125 deaths a day, every day, weekends and holidays included.

A number this large stops meaning anything unless we make it mean something. So start with what each of those deaths actually is: an emptied desk in a classroom, an empty chair at a dinner table, a shift that no one covers. Then multiply it across 46,728 families, and add the classrooms, workplaces, churches and grocery stores where whole communities learned a new set of dates.

It is tempting to treat a toll like this as weather, something that simply happens to the United States. It is not weather. It runs through specific choices, and two of them frame everything else in this brief. Congress chose to let a large share of gun sales proceed with no background check at all, and in 2004 Congress chose to let the assault weapons ban expire. Both choices have a body count attached, and both are reversible.

The annual toll is not a plateau we should learn to live with. It is the running total of a policy failure that has a cure written into it: close the gaps.

## 2. Children and teens

Nowhere is the cost stated more plainly than among children. In 2023, 2,566 children were shot and killed in the United States. That is about seven children every day, a school bus's worth of loss by the end of a week.

Children in America are shot and killed at a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children, ahead of car crashes and every other cause. Read that sentence again, because it has stopped shocking anyone, and it should not. In no other wealthy country is the leading threat to a child's life something that Congress could take off the market.

The usual explanations do not survive contact with the data. American children are not uniquely reckless. Our cities are not uniquely violent. What distinguishes the United States is the sheer availability of guns, including the guns most often used to kill, and availability is a policy choice. Nothing about childhood here requires a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. That number was built, and it can be unbuilt.

Every year that Congress leaves the background check gap and the assault weapons gap open, the tally of children shot and killed starts over. The 2,566 children killed in 2023 will not be in anyone's class photo this fall. Their classmates will carry the absence for the rest of their lives.

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic gate in American gun safety law. Since the Brady law took effect in 1994, anyone buying from a licensed dealer is screened for the disqualifying records federal law already recognizes: felony convictions, domestic violence, and the other categories that Congress has long barred from buying guns.

But the gate only covers some doors, and that is the problem. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged online, at gun shows and between strangers routinely bypass the system entirely. A buyer who would fail a check at a licensed counter can answer an ad, meet a private seller in a parking lot and drive away armed. For someone with a disqualifying record, the workaround is not a hindrance. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks close exactly this gap, and nothing else. The policy is simple: every sale runs through the same system, whoever the seller is. No new categories of prohibited person, no new registry, just the same check applied to every purchase that already carries one when a licensed dealer is involved. It is already law in states across the country, and Congress has debated it for more than a decade without ever closing the gap.

The gap has a cost we can count. Every year it stays open, some share of those 46,728 deaths is a sale that a completed check would have stopped. There is no version of this argument where leaving 40% of the market outside the system is the safer option.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 delivered 656 of them, shootings like Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023. Each of those words is now a place name that stands for a specific afternoon, a specific set of families, and a specific set of unfinished lives.

For the communities that lived through them, nothing here is abstract. And what connects many of the deadliest of these attacks is the weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. # Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
**Northgate Progress Institute**
**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
**October 2026**

## Executive summary

- 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023, one death roughly every 11 minutes. A toll that size is not an accident of American life. It is the product of two gaps in federal law that Congress wrote and that Congress can close.
- 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and they are back on the civilian market.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help states adopt extreme-risk laws. Every one of these steps is ready for a vote.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023. That is one American killed roughly every 11 minutes, around the clock, for an entire year. It is more than 125 deaths a day, every day, weekends and holidays included.

A number this large stops meaning anything unless we make it mean something. So start with what each of those deaths actually is: an emptied desk in a classroom, an empty chair at a dinner table, a shift that no one covers. Then multiply it across 46,728 families, and add the classrooms, workplaces, churches and grocery stores where whole communities learned a new set of dates.

It is tempting to treat a toll like this as weather, something that simply happens to the United States. It is not weather. It runs through specific choices, and two of them frame everything else in this brief. Congress chose to let a large share of gun sales proceed with no background check at all, and in 2004 Congress chose to let the assault weapons ban expire. Both choices have a body count attached, and both are reversible.

The annual toll is not a plateau we should learn to live with. It is the running total of a policy failure that has a cure written into it: close the gaps.

## 2. Children and teens

Nowhere is the cost stated more plainly than among children. In 2023, 2,566 children were shot and killed in the United States. That is about seven children every day, a school bus's worth of loss by the end of a week.

Children in America are shot and killed at a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children, ahead of car crashes and every other cause. Read that sentence again, because it has stopped shocking anyone, and it should not. In no other wealthy country is the leading threat to a child's life something that Congress could take off the market.

The usual explanations do not survive contact with the data. American children are not uniquely reckless. Our cities are not uniquely violent. What distinguishes the United States is the sheer availability of guns, including the guns most often used to kill, and availability is a policy choice. Nothing about childhood here requires a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. That number was built, and it can be unbuilt.

Every year that Congress leaves the background check gap and the assault weapons gap open, the tally of children shot and killed starts over. The 2,566 children killed in 2023 will not be in anyone's class photo this fall. Their classmates will carry the absence for the rest of their lives.

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic gate in American gun safety law. Since the Brady law took effect in 1994, anyone buying from a licensed dealer is screened for the disqualifying records federal law already recognizes: felony convictions, domestic violence, and the other categories that Congress has long barred from buying guns.

But the gate only covers some doors, and that is the problem. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged online, at gun shows and between strangers routinely bypass the system entirely. A buyer who would fail a check at a licensed counter can answer an ad, meet a private seller in a parking lot and drive away armed. For someone with a disqualifying record, the workaround is not a hindrance. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks close exactly this gap, and nothing else. The policy is simple: every sale runs through the same system, whoever the seller is. No new categories of prohibited person, no new registry, just the same check applied to every purchase that already carries one when a licensed dealer is involved. It is already law in states across the country, and Congress has debated it for more than a decade without ever closing the gap.

The gap has a cost we can count. Every year it stays open, some share of those 46,728 deaths is a sale that a completed check would have stopped. There is no version of this argument where leaving 40% of the market outside the system is the safer option.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 delivered 656 of them, shootings like Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023. Each of those words is now a place name that stands for a specific afternoon, a specific set of families, and a specific set of unfinished lives.

For the communities that lived through them, nothing here is abstract. And what connects many of the deadliest of these attacks is the weapon. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. They are designed to put a high volume of fire into human beings quickly, with detachable magazines that let a shooter keep firing while people flee. They have no purpose on a civilian street that justifies what they do in a school hallway.

The country has already run this experiment in the right direction. The 1994 assault weapons ban prohibited the manufacture and sale of these weapons for the civilian market, and it lasted a decade before Congress let it lapse in 2004. Since then the industry has marketed aggressively around the memory of the ban, selling military-style rifles and large-capacity magazines to a civilian customer base, and the results show up in the mass shooting count year after year.

Reinstating the ban is not nostalgia. An updated ban would cover the copycat designs the industry developed to route around the 1994 definitions, and would reach the large-capacity magazines that make these weapons so lethal in crowded places. Congress has the 1994 law as a drafting template and more than two decades of evidence about what the industry did with the gap.

## 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every gun sale, with no exception for private sales, online sales or gun show sales, so that the same standard applies whoever the seller is.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban, extend it to the copycat designs marketed since 2004, and restrict the large-capacity magazines that make these weapons so deadly in crowded places.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, and require that the findings be published so that states and cities can act on them.
4. **Help states adopt extreme-risk laws.** Create grant incentives for state extreme-risk, or red flag, laws that allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove guns from a person in crisis.

The two gaps at the center of this brief were made by Congress. That is the good news, because what Congress made, Congress can unmake. The toll of 2023 is already written into the data.
